steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on GitBug-Actions, a tool that uses GitHub Actions to build reproducible bug-fix benchmarks. Explain why benchmarks need to be recent and reproducible, why CI is a good source of bugs, what the tool does, and list our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Bug-fix benchmarks and why they matter
- Requirement 1: representative / recent bug-fixes
- Requirement 2: reproducibility
- CI systems and GitHub Actions as a source of bug-fixes
- GitBug-Actions: the approach and its proof-of-concept
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Bug-fix benchmarks
  - evaluation resources for SE sub-fields: automatic program repair (APR), fault localization (FL) (cite)
  - definition: modification fixing a defect, aligns behavior with spec; pair of commits = buggy + fixing commit
  - example: Defects4J (cite), widely adopted, served SE research past decade
  - good benchmarks: representative + rigorous
- Representative
  - study relevant problems of today, modern software, not outdated examples
  - modern dev practices, modern languages and build tools
  - recent bugs -> lower risk of data leakage when evaluating LLM techniques (data seen at training time) (cite)
- Reproducible
  - third parties can validate today and in the future
  - fundamental to scientific method, but bug-fix benchmarks fail to retain it over time
  - Zhu and Rubio-González (cite): reproducibility 26.6%–96.9%, none fully reproducible
- CI / GitHub Actions
  - CI systems a valuable source of bug instances (cite)
  - automate build + test -> capture developer-specified environments, bug-fixes collected and reproduced
  - GitHub Actions most popular CI (cite); integrated platform for workflows that build and run test suites
  - key insight: GitHub Actions valuable for high-quality bug-fix benchmarks
- GitBug-Actions
  - novel methodology; identify + run bug-fixes in developer-defined environment
  - collects recent bug-fixes, variety of real-world cases (widespread adoption)
  - fully-reproducible formats: execute locally in workflow environment, store files incl. all dependencies, re-execute offline
  - "executable for eternity"
  - proof-of-concept: Go bug-fixes from January 2023; executable, fully-reproducible, different repositories
- Contributions
  - workflow using GitHub Actions; first to do so
  - public implementation: https://github.com/gitbugactions/gitbugactions
  - proof-of-concept benchmark: 21 fully-reproducible bug-fix commits from 13 repositories

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Bug-fix benchmarks are very important for software engineering research because they give resources to evaluate methods in different sub-fields, like automatic program repair (APR) and fault localization (FL). A bug-fix is a change to the software that fixes an existing defect, so that the program behaves like the intended specification says. It is represented by a pair of commits, a buggy commit and then a fixing commit. For example Defects4J is a bug-fix benchmark that is widely adopted and that has served software engineering research a lot in the past decade. Good benchmarks need to be representative and they need to be rigorous.

First, benchmarks must make sure that the research community studies problems that are relevant today in modern software. Benchmarks should not use outdated examples, they should have bug-fixes that reflect modern development practices and use modern programming languages and build tools. Also, benchmarks with recent bugs reduce the risk of data leakage, which means evaluating large language model (LLM) techniques with data that was seen at training time.

Second, benchmarks have to be reproducible so that third-parties can validate the studies today and also in the future. Reproducibility is fundamental in the scientific method, but bug-fix benchmarks have not been able to keep it over time. For example Zhu and Rubio-González show that the reproducibility of bug-fix benchmarks is between 26.6% and 96.9%, and none of them is fully reproducible.

- CI systems valuable source of bug instances; automate build + test, capture developer-specified environments
- GitHub Actions most popular CI; integrated platform for build/test workflows; key insight: valuable for high-quality benchmarks
- GitBug-Actions: novel methodology, runs bug-fixes in developer-defined environment, collects recent real-world bug-fixes
- fully-reproducible formats: execute locally, store all dependencies, re-execute offline; executable for eternity
- proof-of-concept: Go bug-fixes from January 2023 (executable, fully-reproducible, different repositories)
- Contributions: workflow (first to use GitHub Actions for this); public implementation https://github.com/gitbugactions/gitbugactions; benchmark with 21 bug-fix commits from 13 repositories

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Bug-fix benchmarks are very important for software engineering research because they give resources to evaluate methods in different sub-fields, like automatic program repair (APR) and fault localization (FL). A bug-fix is a change to the software that fixes an existing defect, so that the program behaves like the intended specification says. It is represented by a pair of commits, a buggy commit and then a fixing commit. For example Defects4J is a bug-fix benchmark that is widely adopted and that has served software engineering research a lot in the past decade. Good benchmarks need to be representative and they need to be rigorous.

First, benchmarks must make sure that the research community studies problems that are relevant today in modern software. Benchmarks should not use outdated examples, they should have bug-fixes that reflect modern development practices and use modern programming languages and build tools. Also, benchmarks with recent bugs reduce the risk of data leakage, which means evaluating large language model (LLM) techniques with data that was seen at training time.

Second, benchmarks have to be reproducible so that third-parties can validate the studies today and also in the future. Reproducibility is fundamental in the scientific method, but bug-fix benchmarks have not been able to keep it over time. For example Zhu and Rubio-González show that the reproducibility of bug-fix benchmarks is between 26.6% and 96.9%, and none of them is fully reproducible.

Continuous Integration (CI) systems have been a valuable source of bug instances. CI systems automate the build and the testing, so they capture exactly the environments that developers specified, and bug-fix samples can be collected and reproduced from them. The most popular CI system is GitHub Actions. It gives GitHub users an integrated platform where they define CI workflows that build and execute test suites. Our key insight is that GitHub Actions is a valuable resource for making high-quality bug-fix benchmarks.

In this paper we propose GitBug-Actions, which is a novel methodology to build bug-fix benchmarks based on GitHub Actions. GitBug-Actions uses GitHub Actions to identify bug-fixes and run them in the same environment that the developers defined. Because it uses GitHub Actions, GitBug-Actions collects recent bug-fixes, and these reflect the variety of real-world cases since the CI system is so widely adopted.

GitBug-Actions also keeps the collected bug-fixes in fully-reproducible formats. To do this it executes the bug-fixes locally in the environment that the developers specified in the GitHub Actions workflow, and then it stores the files that are needed, in particular all the software dependencies, so the bug-fixes can be re-executed offline in the same environment. This way the bug-fix benchmarks built by GitBug-Actions uphold scientific standards for reproducibility. The bug-fixes are designed to be executable for eternity.

To validate the concept, we build a proof-of-concept benchmark of Go bug-fixes from January 2023. In total GitBug-Actions collects bug-fixes that are 1) executable, 2) fully-reproducible and 3) from different repositories.

Our contributions are:

- An original workflow for building bug-fix benchmarks with GitHub Actions, called GitBug-Actions. As far as we know we are the first to use GitHub Actions for building bug-fix benchmarks.

- The implementation of GitBug-Actions, which is publicly available so researchers can build benchmarks in their programming language and stack of choice: https://github.com/gitbugactions/gitbugactions.

- A proof-of-concept benchmark of Go bug-fixes from January 2023 collected by GitBug-Actions. It has 21 fully-reproducible bug-fix commits from 13 different repositories.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Bug-fix benchmarks play an important role in advancing software engineering, since they provide essential resources for evaluating methodologies in various sub-fields such as automatic program repair (APR) and fault localization (FL) [1,2]. A bug-fix is a software modification that fixes an existing defect, aligning the program's behavior with the intended specification. It is represented by a pair of commits: a buggy commit and a subsequent fixing commit. For example, Defects4J [3] is a widely adopted bug-fix benchmark that has served software engineering research well in the past decade. Good benchmarks must be representative and rigorous.

First, benchmarks must ensure that the research community studies the relevant problems of today in modern software. Instead of relying on outdated examples, benchmarks must include bug-fixes that reflect modern development practices and that use modern programming languages and build tools. Moreover, benchmarks of recent bugs help reduce the risk of data leakage, i.e. evaluating large language model (LLM) techniques with data seen at training time [4,5].

Second, reproducible benchmarks ensure that such studies can be validated by third-parties today and also in the future. Although reproducibility is fundamental in the scientific method, bug-fix benchmarks have failed to retain it over time. For example, Zhu and Rubio-González [6] show that reproducibility in bug-fix benchmarks varies between 26.6% and 96.9%, with none of them achieving full-reproducibility.

Continuous Integration (CI) systems have been a valuable source of bug instances [7,8]. Since they automate the build and testing processes, CI systems precisely capture the developer-specified environments from which bug-fix samples can be collected and reproduced. GitHub Actions is the most popular CI system [9]. It offers GitHub users an integrated platform for defining CI workflows that build and execute test suites. Our key insight is that GitHub Actions is a valuable resource for creating high-quality bug-fix benchmarks.

In this paper, we propose GitBug-Actions, a novel methodology for building bug-fix benchmarks based on GitHub Actions. GitBug-Actions relies on GitHub Actions to identify bug-fixes and run them in the same environment as the one defined by developers. By using GitHub Actions, GitBug-Actions collects recent bug-fixes that reflect the variety of real-world cases, thanks to the CI system's widespread adoption.

Moreover, GitBug-Actions preserves the collected bug-fixes in fully-reproducible formats. This is done by locally executing the bug-fixes in the environment specified by the developers in the GitHub Actions workflow, and then storing the files needed, in particular all software dependencies, to re-execute the bug-fixes offline in the same environment. In this way, the bug-fix benchmarks built by GitBug-Actions uphold scientific standards w.r.t. reproducibility. The bug-fixes in GitBug-Actions are designed to be executable for eternity.

To validate the concept of GitBug-Actions, we build a proof-of-concept benchmark of Go bug-fixes from January 2023. In total, GitBug-Actions collects bug-fixes that are 1) executable, 2) fully-reproducible and 3) come from different repositories.

To summarize, our contributions are:

- An original workflow for building bug-fix benchmarks using GitHub Actions, called GitBug-Actions. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to use GitHub Actions to build bug-fix benchmarks.

- The implementation of GitBug-Actions, made publicly available for researchers to build benchmarks in their programming language and stack of choice: https://github.com/gitbugactions/gitbugactions.

- A proof-of-concept benchmark of Go bug-fixes from January 2023, collected by GitBug-Actions. The benchmark contains 21 fully-reproducible bug-fix commits from 13 different repositories.
